skill.name: k8s-security-policies
skill.description: Build and review Kubernetes security policies for network isolation, pod security standards, RBAC, admission control, and service mesh authorization.
skill.summary: Guides secure Kubernetes policy design for NetworkPolicy, RBAC, Pod Security Standards, and admission control.

security_audit.summary: Most static alerts are false positives caused by Markdown fences, inline backticks, and Kubernetes policy terminology. One broad egress NetworkPolicy example is confirmed as risky, and additional RBAC examples grant excessive permissions if copied into production. No prompt injection or malicious execution behavior was found.

remediation.suggestion: Replace the 0.0.0.0/0 egress example with named destination CIDRs or document it as a last-resort pattern requiring approval and monitoring.
Use narrow resources and verbs in copyable examples, and move wildcard examples into a clearly labeled anti-pattern section.
Change the secret-reader example to a namespaced Role with resourceNames and only the get verb unless list or watch is strictly required.

finding_verdicts.reason: The metadata endpoint appears in an ipBlock except list with the comment "Block metadata service". This is a defensive NetworkPolicy pattern, not a request to access cloud metadata.

The hardcoded 169.254.169.254/32 address is excluded from allowed egress. Its use reduces metadata exposure rather than creating outbound access to that endpoint.

semantic_findings.title: Overbroad RBAC Wildcard Examples
semantic_findings.description: The RBAC reference includes wildcard resources and verbs in examples tied to production namespaces. Users could copy policies that grant more access than least privilege requires.
semantic_findings.confidence_reasoning: The file directly shows resources ["*"] and verbs ["*"] in named RBAC examples. The surrounding best-practice warning lowers malicious intent, but the copyable production examples remain risky.

semantic_findings.title: Cluster-Wide Secret Read Example
semantic_findings.description: The main guide shows a ClusterRole named secret-reader with get, watch, and list access to secrets. Broad secret visibility can expose credentials if copied into a real cluster.
semantic_findings.confidence_reasoning: The example grants secret access at ClusterRole scope without resourceNames or namespace limits. This is a concrete overprivilege pattern, though it appears educational rather than malicious.

content.value_statement: Kubernetes security policies are difficult to design without overgranting network or API access. This skill provides practical patterns for NetworkPolicy, RBAC, Pod Security Standards, and admission control.
actual_capabilities: Explains namespace labels for Kubernetes Pod Security Standards.
Provides NetworkPolicy patterns for default deny, DNS, ingress, monitoring, and database access.
Shows RBAC Roles, ClusterRoles, RoleBindings, and ServiceAccount patterns.
Includes OPA Gatekeeper constraint examples for required labels.
Describes Istio mTLS and AuthorizationPolicy examples.
Lists kubectl checks for NetworkPolicy and RBAC troubleshooting.
limitations: Does not inspect a live Kubernetes cluster or validate current permissions.
Examples require tailoring before production use.
Does not replace a full CIS Kubernetes Benchmark assessment.
Some examples use broad permissions and need security review before reuse.

use_cases.title: Design namespace isolation
use_cases.description: Create default deny policies and limited service-to-service communication for application namespaces.

use_cases.title: Review RBAC permissions
use_cases.description: Compare roles and bindings against least-privilege goals before deployment.

use_cases.title: Prepare compliance controls
use_cases.description: Map Kubernetes policy patterns to audit logging, pod security, and network segmentation requirements.

prompt_templates.title: Create a default deny baseline
prompt_templates.prompt: Create a default deny NetworkPolicy baseline for my namespace. Include DNS egress and explain what inputs I must customize.

prompt_templates.title: Limit service communication
prompt_templates.prompt: Design NetworkPolicies for a frontend, backend, and database namespace. Allow only required traffic and call out risky assumptions.

prompt_templates.title: Review RBAC for least privilege
prompt_templates.prompt: Review this RBAC design for least privilege. Identify wildcard access, secret exposure, and safer Role or RoleBinding alternatives.

prompt_templates.title: Harden a multi-tenant cluster
prompt_templates.prompt: Build a Kubernetes security policy plan for multiple teams. Cover Pod Security Standards, RBAC, admission control, network isolation, and verification steps.

output_examples.input: Secure a production namespace for one web service and one API service.
output: A default deny baseline for ingress and egress.
A DNS-only egress allowance for pods that need name resolution.
A frontend-to-API rule limited to the required service port.
Verification steps using policy descriptions and connectivity tests.

output_examples.input: Review a service account that can list pods and read one secret.
output: A least-privilege assessment of each permission.
A recommendation to scope secret access by name.
A warning if ClusterRole scope is broader than required.
A short validation checklist for kubectl auth can-i.

output_examples.input: Prepare admission controls for application namespaces.
output: Pod security level recommendations for each namespace.
A rollout sequence with audit, warn, then enforce stages.

best_practices: Start with default deny policies, then add only required ingress and egress paths.
Prefer namespaced Roles with specific resources, verbs, and resourceNames where possible.
Use audit and warning modes before enforcing new admission controls.
anti_patterns: Do not copy wildcard RBAC examples into production without a documented exception.
Do not allow 0.0.0.0/0 egress when a smaller destination set is available.
Do not bind secret-reading permissions at cluster scope unless the use case requires it.

faq.question: Does this skill deploy policies to my cluster?
faq.answer: No. It provides guidance and examples. You must apply and validate changes with your own tooling.

faq.question: Can it help with NetworkPolicy design?
faq.answer: Yes. It covers default deny, DNS egress, service communication, ingress controllers, monitoring, and database access.

faq.question: Does it support modern pod security controls?
faq.answer: Yes. It focuses on Kubernetes Pod Security Standards at the namespace level.

faq.question: Can it review RBAC for risky permissions?
faq.answer: Yes. It can identify broad roles, wildcard permissions, and secret access that need tighter scope.

faq.question: Is it safe to reuse the examples unchanged?
faq.answer: No. Treat the examples as starting points and adapt them to your namespaces, labels, ports, and risk model.

faq.question: Which tools can use this skill?
faq.answer: The report marks support for Claude, Codex, and Claude Code.
